question: Was Georgian Dream's October 26, 2024 parliamentary election victory free and fair?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Government
sideA.text: Georgian Dream won a clear majority (nearly 54%) in an election observed by domestic and some international monitors. The party argues the opposition simply refuses to accept defeat and that fraud claims are a Western-backed pretext to justify unrest, pointing to the absence of any court ruling annulling the results.

sideB.label: Opposition / OSCE-ODIHR / EU
sideB.text: OSCE/ODIHR and independent monitors documented voter intimidation, vote-buying, compromised ballot secrecy and multiple voting at a scale sufficient to affect the outcome. The European Parliament voted 444-72 to reject the election's legitimacy, and President Zourabichvili called it a stolen election orchestrated with Russian interference.

resolution: No independent recount or annulment has occurred; Georgian Dream retains power and the Central Election Commission's results stand as official, but the EU, US and Georgian opposition continue to treat the result as illegitimate.

question: Was the November 2024 suspension of EU accession talks a lawful policy choice or unconstitutional?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Government
sideA.text: The government says it merely postponed the timeline for opening accession negotiations in response to what it calls EU overreach and 'blackmail,' and that the executive retains discretion over the pace of foreign-policy engagement.

sideB.label: Legal Scholars / Opposition / National Bank Staff
sideB.text: Article 78 of Georgia's constitution obligates state institutions to pursue EU and NATO integration; 200 National Bank of Georgia employees and numerous constitutional scholars say the unilateral suspension violates this binding provision without any parliamentary vote or public mandate.

resolution: No court has ruled on the suspension's constitutionality; it remains in force with no accession talks resumed as of mid-2026.

question: Is Mikheil Kavelashvili Georgia's legitimate president?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Government
sideA.text: Kavelashvili was elected under the 2017 constitutional amendments that replaced direct popular election with a 300-member electoral college, a system in force for this cycle; the vote (224 of 225) was procedurally valid.

sideB.label: Salome Zourabichvili / Opposition / EU Parliament
sideB.text: Because the electoral college itself derives its composition from the disputed October 2024 parliamentary election, Zourabichvili and much of the West consider Kavelashvili's mandate tainted at the source and continue to recognize Zourabichvili, or no one, as legitimate head of state.

resolution: Kavelashvili has functioned as president since December 29, 2024, controlling the office in practice, while Zourabichvili and Western governments' informal non-recognition has had no legal effect on his tenure.

question: Is the Foreign Agents Registration Act a transparency measure or a tool of political suppression?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Government
sideA.text: Officials argue the law mirrors the US Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) and simply requires disclosure of foreign funding sources for accountability, applying equally to all organizations regardless of political alignment.

sideB.label: HRW / Amnesty / GYLA / ISFED
sideB.text: Rights groups say the law's criminal penalties, public stigmatization requirements, and selective enforcement against government critics show its real purpose is to dismantle independent civil society and media rather than promote transparency, unlike the US FARA model it claims to mirror.

resolution: The law took effect June 1, 2025; HRW and Amnesty report NGO closures and mass departures through mid-2026, while the government has not prosecuted any pro-government organization under it.

question: Was Mzia Amaglobeli's altercation with police chief Dgebuadze a criminal assault or a defensive reaction to provocation?

sideA.label: Prosecution / Batumi City Court
sideA.text: The court found Amaglobeli guilty of resisting or using violence against a law enforcement officer, initially charging her with a more serious assault offense before reducing it; the conviction reflects an unprovoked physical act against police performing their duties.

sideB.label: Amaglobeli / Press Freedom Groups
sideB.text: Amaglobeli says police chief Dgebuadze insulted her and spat in her face, provoking an instinctive slap during a pro-European protest; CPJ, IFJ and the EU Parliament call the two-year sentence wildly disproportionate and politically motivated retaliation against a prominent independent editor.

resolution: Georgia's Supreme Court declined to hear a further appeal in March 2026, exhausting domestic remedies; the two-year sentence stands and Amaglobeli remains imprisoned.

question: How many political prisoners does Georgia currently hold?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Government
sideA.text: The government does not recognize a 'political prisoner' category, describing all 91 individuals on Transparency International's list as ordinary criminal defendants convicted through due legal process for offenses including violence against police.

sideB.label: Transparency International Georgia / Amnesty International
sideB.text: Applying PACE Resolution 1900 (2012) criteria case-by-case, TI-Georgia counted 91 political prisoners as of July 2026, including protesters, opposition politicians and former Ivanishvili business associates, noting the true count had been higher before some accepted plea deals.

resolution: No independent judicial body has adjudicated the classification; TI-Georgia's figure is the most widely cited by international media and the EU Parliament, while Georgian courts have not overturned any of the underlying convictions en masse.

question: Was the October 4, 2025 attempt to storm the presidential palace a genuine coup attempt or a pretext for a broader crackdown?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Government
sideA.text: Officials describe the storming attempt as an organized effort, backed by opposition figures and foreign-funded groups, to violently overthrow the constitutional order, justifying subsequent legislation enabling party bans and enhanced police powers.

sideB.label: Opposition / International Observers
sideB.text: Opposition figures say the crowd's push toward the palace was a spontaneous escalation of a peaceful mass march by frustrated demonstrators, not a planned coup, and that the government seized on the incident as a pretext to pursue long-planned bans on opposition parties.

resolution: Organizers including Paata Burchuladze face trial on charges of attempting to overthrow the government, carrying up to nine years in prison; the Constitutional Court's party-ban case, filed weeks later citing the unrest, remained pending as of mid-2026.

question: Is the effort to ban the United National Movement, Ahali and Lelo for Georgia a legitimate constitutional process or political persecution?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Government
sideA.text: The government cites Article 23 of the constitution, arguing these parties sought to overthrow constitutional order and undermine Georgia's independence, pointing to the October 4 unrest and years of what it calls destabilizing rhetoric from Saakashvili-aligned figures.

sideB.label: Opposition Parties / Transparency International Georgia
sideB.text: TI-Georgia and opposition leaders call the lawsuit an unprecedented move to eliminate electoral competition entirely, warning that banning the three largest pro-EU parties would leave Georgia a de facto one-party state ahead of any future election.

resolution: The Constitutional Court had not ruled as of mid-2026; Parliament's speaker suggested a decision could come by July 2026, and Georgian Dream expanded the lawsuit in March 2026 to include the Federalists party.

question: Has Georgian law enforcement used excessive, systemic force against protesters, and has anyone been held accountable?

sideA.label: Ministry of Internal Affairs
sideA.text: The ministry maintains that force used against demonstrators was proportionate responses to violent or illegal assembly, and that any individual misconduct allegations are investigated through normal disciplinary channels.

sideB.label: Public Defender's Office / Amnesty International
sideB.text: The Ombudsman documented that 78–88% of detainees in 2024–2025 reported ill-treatment, with hundreds showing visible injuries; Amnesty's 2026 report found authorities have 'consistently failed' to hold any police officer accountable despite the scale of documented abuse.

resolution: No senior police or ministry official has been prosecuted for crackdown-related abuses as of mid-2026, even as 49 officers resigned in December 2024 citing orders from leadership.

question: Did the October 2025 municipal elections represent a legitimate mandate for Georgian Dream given the boycott?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Government
sideA.text: The government points to a clean sweep of all 64 municipalities and a 41% turnout as evidence of continued public support, arguing the opposition boycott was a self-defeating strategic error rather than a sign of the vote's illegitimacy.

sideB.label: Opposition Parties / Carnegie Endowment
sideB.text: Boycotting opposition parties argue participating would have legitimized what they call a Russian-backed regime; analysts note turnout fell ten points from 2021 and warn the boycott handed Georgian Dream uncontested control it then used to justify further crackdowns, including the party-ban lawsuit.

resolution: Georgian Dream governs all 64 municipalities uncontested; the boycott strategy is widely viewed, including by some opposition figures, as having backfired by removing checks on the ruling party rather than delegitimizing it in practice.

question: Is Georgia's warming relationship with Russia pragmatic economic policy or evidence of state capture by Moscow-aligned interests?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Government
sideA.text: Officials frame resumed direct flights, visa-free travel and growing trade with Russia as pragmatic normalization benefiting Georgian businesses and citizens, distinct from any political alignment, while insisting Georgia's occupied territories remain a core national concern.

sideB.label: Opposition / Western Analysts
sideB.text: Critics point to Ivanishvili's 'global war party' conspiracy rhetoric, the EU accession freeze, NATO's suspension of cooperation programs, and bilateral trade climbing to $2.69 billion in 2025 as evidence of a broader strategic tilt away from the West and toward accommodation with the Kremlin.

resolution: Trade and travel ties with Russia have expanded steadily since 2023 even as EU/NATO integration has stalled; Georgia has not recognized Abkhazia or South Ossetia's occupation status, but normalization with Moscow continues on other fronts.

question: Does Bidzina Ivanishvili control the Georgian government despite holding no formal office?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Ivanishvili
sideA.text: Ivanishvili holds the ceremonial title of Honorary Chairman of Georgian Dream and denies directing government policy, saying decisions are made by elected officials including PM Kobakhidze and President Kavelashvili.

sideB.label: Opposition / US State Department
sideB.text: The US sanctioned Ivanishvili by name in December 2024, stating he personally 'derailed Georgia's Euro-Atlantic future'; opposition figures and Western analysts describe him as the party's undisputed de facto leader whose speeches set policy direction, including the anti-Western 'global war party' narrative.

resolution: Ivanishvili remains formally outside government office but is widely treated by Western governments, protest organizers and independent analysts as Georgian Dream's ultimate decision-maker; he faces US but not (due to Hungarian/Slovak vetoes) EU sanctions.

question: Is Georgia's growing isolation from NATO and the EU self-inflicted or the result of double standards from the West?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Government
sideA.text: Officials say NATO and EU institutions have applied inconsistent standards to Georgia compared to other candidate countries, and that Western criticism reflects a preference for a compliant government rather than genuine concern about democratic standards.

sideB.label: European Commission / NATO / Opposition
sideB.text: The European Commission has repeatedly called Georgia 'a candidate country in name only' and demanded it 'urgently reverse democratic backsliding'; NATO suspended 5 of 17 cooperation programs and excluded Georgia from its 2026 summit citing the foreign-influence laws and political crackdown as the direct cause.

resolution: Georgia's EU accession remains frozen and NATO cooperation curtailed as of mid-2026, with both bodies explicitly linking the isolation to the government's own legislative and law-enforcement record rather than external factors.

question: Are Mikheil Saakashvili's convictions legitimate prosecutions of past abuses of power or political vendetta?

sideA.label: Prosecutor's Office / Government
sideA.text: Prosecutors say the cumulative roughly 12.5-year sentence reflects legitimate convictions for abuse of office, embezzlement and illegal return to Georgia, addressing conduct from Saakashvili's 2004–2012 presidency that predates Georgian Dream's rule.

sideB.label: United National Movement / International Rights Groups
sideB.text: Saakashvili's supporters and several Western governments call the prosecutions politically motivated retaliation against Georgian Dream's chief political rival, pointing to his deteriorating health, repeated hunger strikes, and restrictive hospital detention as evidence of mistreatment beyond any legitimate penal purpose.

resolution: Saakashvili remains imprisoned with a cumulative sentence extending years into the future; no international court has ruled on the underlying convictions' legitimacy.

question: Does the Broadcasting Law's foreign-funding ban protect Georgian media sovereignty or destroy independent journalism?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / Communications Commission
sideA.text: Officials argue foreign grants have historically been used to steer Georgian broadcasters toward a pro-opposition editorial line, and that banning such funding — while allowing narrow exceptions for non-political specialty channels — restores media independence from outside political influence.

sideB.label: CPJ / IFJ / Independent Broadcasters
sideB.text: Press-freedom groups say most independent Georgian outlets have relied on foreign grants for years given the small domestic ad market, and that the law's real effect is to defund and criminalize the only media still reporting critically on the government.

resolution: By mid-2026, CPJ and HRW reported independent outlets closing or shrinking under the funding ban, while the government moved to allow foreign funding again only for non-political specialty channels such as sports and entertainment.

question: Is Irakli Garibashvili's 'trap' allegation a genuine break with Ivanishvili or a bid for leniency?

sideA.label: Georgian Dream / PM Kobakhidze
sideA.text: Kobakhidze dismissed Garibashvili's Facebook statements as 'problematic,' pointing out that Garibashvili already admitted guilt under his January 2026 plea deal and suggesting the claims are a self-serving attempt to relitigate a settled case rather than a credible account of government pressure.

sideB.label: Garibashvili / Independent Analysts
sideB.text: Garibashvili says he was ordered, via a letter sent on Ivanishvili's instructions, to plead guilty to a new corruption charge and permanently exit politics, and that officials threatened to arrest his elderly father; analysts note this is the first time a former Ivanishvili loyalist has publicly broken ranks, suggesting real strain inside Georgian Dream's inner circle.

resolution: On Aug 24, 2026, prosecutors filed a further bribery charge against Garibashvili carrying 11-15 years, days after his public break with Ivanishvili; his lawyers say he denies guilt and will contest it, while PM Kobakhidze dismissed his allegations as 'problematic.' No independent body has verified the alleged pressure, and the new charge's timing is itself now part of the dispute over whether the case is retaliatory.
